title: Sustained turbo budgets, KV eviction, and kernel throttling — guidance and heuristics
content:
Summary:
This note captures a pragmatic set of heuristics and rollout guidance for combining sustained-turbo (long-term boost) budgeting with KV cache eviction policies and kernel throttling/fallback logic across our GPU fleet (NVIDIA A100/H100, NVIDIA L4, AMD MI300). The goal is to reduce tail latency regressions and thermal/power-driven fallback events while minimizing end-to-end cost/perf impact for production inference.

Why this matters (motivation):
- We observe occasional model-quality regressions or latency spikes when GPUs enter prolonged thermal/power-limited modes (sustained-power reduction). Those events interact badly with large KV caches (memory pressure + eviction churn) and runtime kernel choices (precision/tiling).
- Rolling out conservative per-GPU power budgets without KV/kernel coordination causes unexpected throughput drops or increased token costs, since eviction churn increases memory traffic and kernel fallbacks raise per-token latency.

High-level goals:
1) Provide a small set of per-device sustained-turbo budget recommendations (power headroom and duration) for stable inference.
2) Define KV-cache eviction thresholds and retention priorities that respect transient power-mode transitions.
3) Implement kernel fallback rules that prefer degrading precision or batch packing before evicting hot KV entries when possible.
4) Give a safe rollout checklist and telemetry signals to detect negative regressions.

Assumptions and constraints: 
- We target production LLM workloads with mixed sequence-length distributions and variable arrival rates (microbursts common).
- Dedicated pools can accept slightly higher sustained budgets than shared-hosted GPUs.
- KV cache is per-model with configurable phys memory quotas; eviction should be bounded to avoid cascading KV reloads.
- We prioritize tail latency (95–99 pct) and cost per token as primary metrics.

Key telemetry signals to expose (runtime & node):
- sustained_power_limit_watts (current enforced cap), recent history (1m/5m/1h)
- gpu_clock_mhz and sm_clock_percentile (p95/p50/p5)
- power_throttle_events and thermal_throttle_events (counts and timestamps)
- gpu_mem_used_bytes vs cache_quota_bytes and mem_pressure_ratio (mem_used/total_memory)
- kv_eviction_rate_per_min and avg_evicted_kv_size_bytes
- kernel_fallback_count_by_reason (precision/tiling/memory)
- per-request latency percentiles and token-per-second throughput by model-version

Heuristic rules (runtime side):
1) Sustained budget detection and labeling
   - Detect when a GPU has applied a sustained power cap (external policy or automatic DVFS) for >30s and label the node "sustained-capped".
   - If sustained-capped persists beyond 5 minutes, transition to "sustained-degraded" for routing decisions.

2) KV eviction policy tied to power state
   - Baseline behavior (no cap): LRU with size and recency weighted by requests.
   - When node labeled sustained-capped: raise the eviction threshold conservatively by +10–20% (free more memory earlier) but only evict cold shards first (eviction_score = alpha * recency + beta * fetch_count; increase alpha weight when capped).
   - Add a protected set: the top-N most-recently-accessed KV pages (or percentage of quota) must not be evicted during first 60s of a cap event unless mem_pressure_ratio > 0.9. This avoids re-load storms.

3) Kernel throttling and fallback precedence
   - Kernel fallback should be stepwise with clear precedence: (1) reduce batch packing/merge small requests to reduce memory pressure, (2) enable lower-precision kernel (FP16 -> TF32 fallback reversed; prefer FP16/AMP for LLM where validated), (3) switch to quantized/int8 kernel if model validated, (4) as last resort, destroy some large KV segments to free memory.
   - Each fallback step must have a small hysteresis window (30–120s) and a maximum allowed frequency (e.g., at most one full fallback cycle per 5m) to avoid oscillation.

4) Scheduling interactions
   - Scheduler should prefer spreading hot-keyed models across multiple GPUs to avoid concentrated mem pressure when a sustained cap hits one machine.
   - For mixed-criticality tenants, prefer routing latency-SLO-critical requests away from nodes in "sustained-degraded" state.

Per-hardware recommended starting budgets and notes (empirical guidance, needs lab validation):
- NVIDIA A100 (40/80GB):
  - Suggested sustained budget: 250–300W for 80GB SXM, 200–230W for 40GB PCIe under latency-sensitive workloads.
  - Rationale: A100s have wide thermal envelope; moderate sustained capping reduces peak power while preserving SM clock headroom.
  - KV guidance: keep KV quota to <= 70% of device RAM in shared pools; protect top-10% hot pages.
  - Kernel notes: A100 benefits from FP16 kernels; prefer cuBLAS/cuDNN frontend that uses Tensor Cores. Fallback to tf32 only if memory spikes persist.

- NVIDIA H100: 
  - Suggested sustained budget: 280–320W for SXM (latency-critical), 220–260W for lower-cost modes.
  - Rationale: H100 delivers higher throughput but is more sensitive to frequency scaling for certain attention kernels. Keep a slightly higher sustained cap than A100 to avoid kernel slowdowns.
  - KV guidance: H100 memory is high-throughput; safe to allow KV up to 75% in dedicated pools, but protect hot entries more aggressively.
  - Kernel notes: H100 benefits from tensor op optimizations; kernel fallback to lower tile sizes first (avoid full precision fallback if possible).

- NVIDIA L4 (edge/VM-gpu):
  - Suggested sustained budget: 70–100W depending on VM class and thermal headroom.
  - Rationale: L4s are small-memory / efficient; memory pressure is the typical failure mode.
  - KV guidance: cap KV quota conservatively (<=50–60%); use very small protected sets (top 3–5%).
  - Kernel notes: Favor INT8/quantized kernels for throughput; ensure model quality A/B tests before enabling.

- AMD MI300: 
  - Suggested sustained budget: 350–420W (MI300X-class) tuned per chassis; MI300 may have different DVFS characteristics.
  - Rationale: MI300 has wide memory bandwidth but different clock/power tradeoffs; monitor memory temperature metrics if exposed.
  - KV guidance: MI300 can sustain larger KV quotas in dedicated capacity; still use protected set semantics during capping windows.
  - Kernel notes: Ensure ROCm kernels have quantized paths tested; fallback sequence similar to NVIDIA but use vendor-optimized routines where available.

Operational rollout checklist (safe steps):
1) Lab validation (staging cluster): run representative models (chat, completion, embeddings/long-seq) and simulate sustained caps at target wattages for 10m windows. Track kv_eviction_rate, kernel_fallback_count, p95/p99 latency.
2) Canary: enable cap + policies for 5% of capacity for non-latency-critical tenants for 48–72 hours. Watch errors and cost.
3) Expand: 25% capacity for 1 week; if regressions < threshold (p95 increase <5%, kv reload cost <8%), proceed.
4) Fleet-wide: rolling enable with routing rules to keep critical traffic off nodes labelled sustained-degraded.

Telemetry and alerting thresholds suggestions:
- kv_eviction_rate_per_min > 200 -> alert to infra (eviction storm).
- kernel_fallback_count_by_reason["precision"] > 5/min -> investigate power/thermal events.
- sustained-degraded nodes > 10% of pool -> automatic scaling trigger or routing shift.
- p99 latency regression > 15% over baseline for a model -> rollback caps for affected node class.

Experiments to run (prioritized):
1) Eviction protection size vs reload cost: sweep protected_set from 3% -> 20% and measure reload token cost and p99 latency under sustained cap.
2) Fallback order ablation: compare performance & quality when lowering precision before shrinking KV vs shrinking KV first.
3) Short microburst tolerance: measure how microburst frequency and batching policies interact with handled caps (simulate traffic spikes).
4) Per-model sensitivity matrix: run common models under each hardware cap and record degradation curves (latency & quality).

Open questions / risks: 
- How to reliably attribute kernel fallback events to power/throttle vs memory fragmentation? Need finer-grained kernel telemetry.
- Interplay with host-level cgroups / container memory limits — eviction semantics may differ.
- Quantized kernels may produce small quality regressions; need model-specific QA.

Implementation notes and API hooks: 
- Expose node label and recent power-cap history in the scheduler API so routing decisions can be made externally.
- KV manager: add a "protected_set" config (percent or count) + dynamic alpha/beta weights influenced by node state.
- Kernel manager: implement a state machine with backoff timers and counters to cap fallback frequency. Record reason codes in metrics (power, memory, tile-size).

Appendix: quick reference (one-line):
- If node enters sustained cap: raise KV eviction aggressiveness by 10–20%, protect top hot pages for 60s, prefer precision downgrade before evicting hot KV, and avoid routing SLO-critical traffic there after 5m.

Contact for questions: Ava Chen (owner), eng-serving-runtime slack #serving-runtime.

Notes: this is a pragmatic, rollout-first doc — not final. Please use the lab experiment matrix and update numbers after validation.
